Windows of Heaven
WIN-dohz uv HEV-un
n. phr. (the openings of the sky, used of the flood and of overwhelming blessing)
Hebrew arubboth ha-shamayim — arubbah, a lattice, sluice, or window, from a root meaning to lie in wait or to be latticed; and shamayim, the heavens.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

The phrase is used in Scripture of judgment and of blessing, and the same figure serves both. At the flood: “the same day were all the fountains of the great deep broken up, and the windows of heaven were opened,” and when the judgment is finished, “The fountains also of the deep and the windows of heaven were stopped, and the rain from heaven was restrained.” The imagery is of latticed openings in the sky that God unbars and bars again, and the pairing with the fountains of the deep means the flood came from above and below at once — a deliberate undoing of the second day's separation of the waters. Malachi turns the same figure to mercy in the one passage where God invites His people to test Him: “Bring ye all the tithes into the storehouse… and prove me now herewith, saith the LORD of hosts, if I will not open you the windows of heaven, and pour you out a blessing, that there shall not be room enough to receive it.” A third occurrence is a warning about unbelief. When Elisha promised plenty in a besieged and starving Samaria, a lord on whose hand the king leaned answered, “Behold, if the LORD would make windows in heaven, might this thing be?” The prophet's reply is exact: “thou shalt see it with thine eyes, but shalt not eat thereof.” The man used the figure to mock a promise, and was granted the sight and denied the supper.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828): Window, an opening in a wall for the admission of light. The windows of heaven, Genesis 7:11, the openings of the sky, used both of the flood and of overflowing blessing.

expand to see more

Window, an opening in the wall of a building for the admission of light.

Hebrew arubbah, a lattice, a sluice, a window or opening.

The windows of heaven were opened, Genesis 7:11, at the flood.

The windows of heaven were stopped, Genesis 8:2, when it was stayed.

Open you the windows of heaven, and pour you out a blessing, Malachi 3:10.

Key Scripture

Gen 7:11 — "In the six hundredth year of Noah's life, in the second month, the seventeenth day of the month, the same day were all the fountains of the great deep broken up, and the windows of heaven were opened."

Gen 8:2 — "The fountains also of the deep and the windows of heaven were stopped, and the rain from heaven was restrained;"

Mal 3:10 — "Bring ye all the tithes into the storehouse, that there may be meat in mine house, and prove me now herewith, saith the LORD of hosts, if I will not open you the windows of heaven, and pour you out a blessing, that there shall not be room enough to receive it."

2Ki 7:2 — "Then a lord on whose hand the king leaned answered the man of God, and said, Behold, if the LORD would make windows in heaven, might this thing be? And he said, Behold, thou shalt see it with thine eyes, but shalt not eat thereof."

Modern Corruption

Malachi 3:10 has been detached from its covenant setting and made the proof text of prosperity preaching, in which giving is an investment technique and the windows open on demand.

expand to see more

The prosperity gospel rests more weight on this verse than on almost any other, and the handling is consistently dishonest in three ways. It is addressed to the covenant nation under the Mosaic law, in a specific moment of national robbery of the storehouse, and the blessing named is agricultural — the rebuking of the devourer and the fruitfulness of the vine. It is not a promise of financial return to individual donors, and still less to donors giving to the preacher who quotes it. The movement then inverts the verse's logic: Malachi's invitation to prove God is a rebuke to a people who were withholding, whereas the prosperity use turns it into a technique by which God's hand is moved, which makes the Almighty a mechanism and the giver the one in control.

The New Testament's own teaching on giving stands against the scheme without discouraging generosity, which is the balance to keep. Paul does promise that he who sows bountifully shall reap bountifully, but the reaping he names is grace sufficient for every good work, and he insists the giver purpose it in his heart, not grudgingly nor of necessity. Meanwhile the flood occurrences keep the figure honest. The same windows that pour out blessing poured out the waters that drowned the world, and the Samaritan lord who treated the phrase as a sarcasm about what God could not do was given exactly what he asked for and none of what he needed. The principle to recover is that heaven's openings are at God's discretion and not at man's disposal.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew arubbah, a lattice or sluice, hence a window; shamayim, the heavens; openings that God unbars for judgment or for blessing.

expand to see more

Hebrew arubbah, a lattice, a sluice, a window or opening.

Hebrew shamayim, the heavens, plural in form.

Opened at the flood together with the fountains of the great deep.

Stopped when the judgment was stayed, Genesis 8:2.

Turned to blessing in the one invitation to prove God, Malachi 3:10.
